title: Exploring at random
objectives: Build an epsilon-greedy agent with running means, and explain the regret it cannot avoid.

screens.title: One order in ten
screens.prose: Greedy locked onto a worse venue in 127 of 200 seeds. A simple cure: send 1 order in 10 to a venue picked uniformly at random, and the rest to the current favourite. The venues fill with chance 0.45, 0.55 and 0.60.
screens.question: Suppose the favourite is already C, the best venue. What regret do the random orders still cost per 1,000 orders? Give a decimal to 2 places.

hints.text: About 100 of the 1,000 orders go to a random venue.
A random pick can land on A, B or C, so it loses $0.60 - 0.5333$ on average.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out the average loss of one random order, then count the random orders.

byKey.no-c: You left C out of the random pick. A uniform pick lands on C a third of the time, and that costs nothing.
byKey.all-random: That is the regret if every order were random. Only 1 in 10 is.
byKey.all-lost: You charged each random order C's whole fill chance, 0.60. It loses only the gap to C on average.

explain.text: A random order loses $0.60 - \tfrac{1.6}{3} = 0.0667$ on average. About 100 orders in 1,000 are random, so the cost is 6.67 fills. No amount of learning removes it.

screens.title: Four settings of the dial
screens.prose: Call the share of random orders $\varepsilon$. We ran the agent 200 times for each of four values on the three venues, with seeds 0 to 199. The lines are the mean regret so far. Slide to draw them.
screens.question: Which $\varepsilon$ has the lowest mean regret after 1,000 orders?

options.why: With no random orders the agent can lock onto A or B for good. Its line ends highest, near 56.
One order in 100 is too few to escape a bad lock early. Its line ends near 41.
It escapes locks quickly but then keeps paying for 3 random orders in 10. Its line ends near 30.

feedback.generic: Slide to the end and read where each line stops.

explain.text: The recorded means at 1,000 orders are 56.0, 40.6, 24.0 and 30.0 for $\varepsilon$ = 0, 0.01, 0.1 and 0.3. The 0.3 line is nearly straight: it keeps paying for its random orders. The $\varepsilon$ = 0 line is plain greedy with a different random stream: its 56.0 and the 61.8 quoted for greedy later differ only by noise.

screens.title: Epsilon-greedy and its floor
screens.prose: This agent is **epsilon-greedy**: with chance $\varepsilon$ it pulls a uniformly random arm, otherwise the arm with the best estimate. Its random pulls lose $q^* - \bar q$ each on average, where $\bar q$ is the mean of the arm values. So its regret per pull never falls below $\varepsilon\,(q^* - \bar q)$.
screens.question: What is the floor on the regret of $\varepsilon = 0.3$ over 1,000 orders?

hints.text: The floor per pull is $\varepsilon$ times the average loss of a random pull.
The average loss is $0.60 - 0.5333 = 0.0667$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Multiply the orders, $\varepsilon$ and the average loss of a random pull.

byKey.eps01: That is the floor for $\varepsilon = 0.1$. This agent explores three times as often.
byKey.no-eps: You left out $\varepsilon$: only 3 orders in 10 are random.
byKey.per-pull: That is the floor per order. Multiply by the 1,000 orders.

explain.text: The floor is $1000 \times 0.3 \times 0.0667 = 20$ fills, the dashed line. The recorded mean, 30.0, sits above it: the extra 10 is what the agent lost while learning.

screens.title: Code the agent
screens.prose: Each step, draw `rng.random()` first. Below `eps`, explore with `a = rng.randrange(len(ps))`; otherwise `a = argmax_random(Q, rng)`. Then pull and update with `Q[a] += (r - Q[a]) / n[a]`. Draw `rng.random()` even when `eps` is 0, so the seeded stream stays in step. Then write `regret_floor(ps, eps)`.
screens.question: Complete `epsilon_greedy` and `regret_floor`.

widget.how: Submit runs 8 hidden tests. Totals must equal ours exactly, so draw `rng.random()` first every step; floors are compared with `math.isclose`.

mutants.symptom: Random pulls skip the current best arm, so the stream and the floor change.
Floor taken as eps times the gap to the worst arm.
No draw when eps is 0, so the seeded stream shifts.

hints.text: The only change from greedy is how `a` is chosen.
`if rng.random() < eps:` explore, `else:` exploit.
The floor is `eps * (max(ps) - sum(ps) / len(ps))`.

feedback.correct: Both pass. The floor for the venues at 0.1 is 0.00667 a pull, 6.67 per 1,000.
feedback.generic: Some tests fail. Check that `rng.random()` is drawn first on every step, then the arm, then the pull.

explain.text: The explore branch uses `rng.randrange`, the exploit branch `argmax_random`, and both then pull. The floor is $\varepsilon(q^* - \bar q)$, which is $0.1 \times 0.0667 = 0.00667$ here.

screens.title: Turning the dial down
screens.prose: The floor comes from exploring at the same rate for ever. Exploring is worth most early, when the estimates are poor. So let the rate fall: $\varepsilon_t = 1/\sqrt{t}$ on pull $t$. The first pull is always random; pull 100 is random with chance 0.1.
screens.question: How many random pulls does $\varepsilon_t = 1/\sqrt{t}$ make on average in the first 1,000 pulls? Give a decimal to 1 place.

hints.text: The expected count is the sum of the chances.
Add $1/\sqrt{t}$ for $t = 1$ to $1000$.
The sum is close to $2\sqrt{1000} - 1.46$. Work it out to 1 place.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the chance of a random pull over every $t$ from 1 to 1,000.

byKey.fixed: That is the count for a fixed $\varepsilon = 0.1$. The decaying rate explores less after pull 100.
byKey.root: That is $\sqrt{1000}$. The sum of $1/\sqrt t$ grows like $2\sqrt T$.
byKey.last: That is the chance on the last pull only. Add the chances of all 1,000 pulls.

explain.text: The expected number of random pulls is $\sum_{t=1}^{1000} t^{-1/2} = 61.8$. The share of random pulls now falls towards 0, so the fixed floor is gone. Rates that fall too fast bring back the risk of locking in.

screens.title: Optimism at the start
screens.prose: A second cheap trick needs no random pulls. Start every estimate at 1, as if each arm had already won once, so $n$ starts at 1. Greedy then tries each arm until its estimate falls. Over 200 seeds this agent's mean regret was 27.9, against 61.8 for plain greedy.
screens.question: Arm A starts at $Q = 1$ with $n = 1$ and loses its first two real pulls. What is its estimate now? Give a decimal to 4 places.

hints.text: The pretend win counts as one reward in the mean.
After two losses the mean is over 3 rewards: 1, 0, 0.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Average the pretend win with the two real losses.

byKey.real-only: You dropped the starting 1. It counts as one reward until it is outweighed.
byKey.half: You halved twice. The running mean is $(1 + 0 + 0)/3$, not $1 \times \tfrac12 \times \tfrac12$.
byKey.one-loss: That is after one loss. A second loss brings it to a third.

explain.text: The running mean of 1, 0, 0 is 0.3333. An untried arm still shows 1, so greedy moves on to it. Every arm gets tried early, which is why regret falls from 61.8 to 27.9.

screens.title: When the venue changes
screens.prose: Venue C fills with chance 0.60 for 500 orders, then 0.40. The sample mean weighs every reward equally, so it moves slowly. A constant step $\alpha$ updates $Q \leftarrow Q + \alpha(R - Q)$: an exponentially weighted mean. One seeded run, $\alpha = 0.1$:
screens.question: With $\alpha = 0.1$, what total weight do rewards from before the drop carry 20 pulls after it? Give a decimal to 4 places.

hints.text: Each update keeps $1 - \alpha$ of the old estimate.
After 20 updates the old estimate is scaled by $0.9^{20}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Each update multiplies the weight on the old estimate by 0.9.

byKey.linear: You let the old rewards drop out after 10 steps. The weight shrinks by 0.9 a step but never reaches 0.
byKey.one-step: That is after one pull. Twenty pulls scale it by $0.9^{20}$.
byKey.new-weight: That is the weight on the 20 new rewards. The question asks about the old ones.

explain.text: The old estimate keeps $0.9^{20} = 0.1216$ of its weight, so $\alpha = 0.1$ tracks the drop within a few dozen orders. The sample mean is still 0.50 after 1,000 orders, halfway between the two chances. Use a constant step when an arm can change.

screens.title: A constant step
screens.prose: Write `ewma_update(q, r, alpha)`, the update with a constant step. It is the running mean with $\tfrac1n$ replaced by $\alpha$: new estimate = old + step × error once more. After 30 wins from 0 with $\alpha = 0.1$ the estimate is $1 - 0.9^{30} = 0.9576$.
screens.question: Complete `ewma_update`.

widget.how: Submit runs 6 hidden tests. Each result is compared with `math.isclose`.

mutants.symptom: Replaces the estimate by the reward.

hints.text: The error is `r - q`.
Move a fraction `alpha` of the error.
`return q + alpha * (r - q)`.

feedback.correct: It passes. With $\alpha = 1$ the estimate jumps to the last reward; small $\alpha$ moves it slowly.
feedback.generic: Some tests fail. Return the old estimate plus `alpha` times the error.

explain.text: `q + alpha * (r - q)` keeps $1 - \alpha$ of the old estimate. Rewards $k$ steps old carry weight $\alpha(1 - \alpha)^k$, so old evidence fades.

screens.title: Is more exploring safer?
screens.prose: Two desks run epsilon-greedy on the three venues for 10,000 orders. Desk X uses $\varepsilon = 0.1$; desk Y uses $\varepsilon = 0.3$ "to be safe". Both have found C after the first 1,000 orders.

state.caption: The floors over 10,000 orders fill in after you answer.

screens.question: Which desk can expect the lower regret over the 10,000 orders?

options.text: X: its floor is 66.7 fills, Y's is 200
Y: exploring more is always the safer choice
options.why: Y explores three times as often for all 10,000 orders. Each random order costs 0.0667 on average, so its floor is three times higher.

options.text: Neither: once C is found the two are level
options.why: Finding C does not stop the random orders. They keep costing at the rate $\varepsilon$ sets.

options.text: Y, because it found C sooner than X
options.why: Both found C in the first 1,000 orders. After that only the random orders differ.

hints.text: After C is found, regret comes from the random orders.
The floor per order is $\varepsilon \times 0.0667$.
X: $10000 \times 0.1 \times 0.0667$. Y: three times that.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the cost of the random orders that continue after C is found.

byKey.y: You chose more exploring as the safe option. Past the first lock-ins it is a steady cost that grows with $\varepsilon$.

explain.text: Over 10,000 orders the floors are $10000 \times 0.1 \times 0.0667 = 66.7$ for X and $10000 \times 0.3 \times 0.0667 = 200$ for Y. More exploring helps early but costs for ever. The bars show the two floors.

screens.title: The rules so far
screens.prose: Epsilon-greedy explores with chance $\varepsilon$, so its regret per pull is at least $$\varepsilon\,(q^* - \bar q).$$ A falling $\varepsilon_t$ or optimistic starting values cut that cost. For an arm that can change, a constant step $$Q \leftarrow Q + \alpha(R - Q)$$ gives a reward $k$ steps old the weight $\alpha(1 - \alpha)^k$.
screens.question: Which arm needs a constant step $\alpha$ rather than the step $\tfrac1n$?

options.text: An arm whose value can change over time
An arm that has been pulled only a few times
options.why: For a few pulls, $\tfrac1n$ is large anyway. The constant step matters when old rewards stop being relevant.

options.text: The arm with the highest value so far
options.why: Which arm is best does not decide the step. Whether its value can move does.

options.text: Every arm, in every bandit problem
options.why: For an arm that never changes, $\tfrac1n$ gives the exact sample mean, which is better.

feedback.correct: A constant step forgets old rewards, which suits an arm whose value moves.
feedback.generic: Ask which arm has rewards that go out of date.

screens.title: Keeping a backup venue warm
screens.prose: A desk routes 200,000 orders a month. Its main venue fills with chance 0.62 and a backup with 0.58. It always sends 5% of orders to the backup, so it notices if the two ever swap. A lost fill costs £1.50.
screens.question: While the main venue stays best, what does the 5% cost each month, in pounds?

hints.text: Only the orders sent to the backup lose anything.
Each loses $0.62 - 0.58 = 0.04$ fills on average.
$200000 \times 0.05 \times 0.04$ fills, at £1.50 each.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the backup orders, multiply by the gap, then price the lost fills.

byKey.fills: That is the cost in fills. Price each at £1.50.
byKey.all-backup: You charged the gap on every order. Only 5% go to the backup.
byKey.whole-fill: You counted each backup order as a whole lost fill. It loses only the 0.04 gap on average.

explain.text: The backup gets 10,000 orders a month, each 0.04 fills short of the main venue: 400 fills, or £600. That is the price of noticing within weeks if the venues swap, which a desk that never explores would miss.

ideas: Epsilon-greedy pulls a random arm with chance $\varepsilon$, otherwise its best estimate. A little exploring escapes the lock-ins that sink greedy.
Its random pulls cost $\varepsilon(q^* - \bar q)$ per pull for ever: a floor that grows with $\varepsilon$. A falling $\varepsilon_t$ or optimistic starting values lower it.
For an arm whose value can change, a constant step $Q \leftarrow Q + \alpha(R - Q)$ forgets old rewards at rate $1 - \alpha$ per pull.

formula.name: Regret floor of epsilon-greedy
formula.note: For a fixed $\varepsilon$ and uniform exploration; $\bar q$ is the mean of the arm values.

summary.trap: More exploring is not always safer: past the first lock-ins every random pull is a steady cost, three times higher at $\varepsilon = 0.3$ than at 0.1.

quiz.prose: Four arms win with chance 0.2, 0.4, 0.5 and 0.7. An agent explores with $\varepsilon = 0.2$.
quiz.question: What is its floor on regret per pull? Give a decimal to 3 places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Average the four values, then take the gap to 0.7 and scale by $\varepsilon$.

byKey.no-eps: That is the loss of one random pull. Only a fifth of pulls are random.
byKey.worst: You used the worst arm's gap, 0.5. A random pull loses the average gap.

explain.text: A random pull loses $0.7 - 0.45 = 0.25$ on average. A fifth of pulls are random, so the floor is 0.05 per pull.

quiz.prose: An estimate is 0.4. With $\alpha = 0.2$ the next two rewards are 1 and 1.
quiz.question: What is the estimate after both? Give a decimal to 3 places.

byKey.one: That is after one reward. Apply the update again.
byKey.mean: You averaged the three numbers. A constant step moves only a fifth of the way each time.

quiz.prose: An epsilon-greedy agent with $\varepsilon = 0.05$ has pulled each arm hundreds of times.
quiz.question: Why does it keep exploring at all?

options.text: Its rule explores at a fixed rate whatever it has learned
It is still unsure which arm is best
options.why: Epsilon-greedy never measures its own uncertainty. It explores at the fixed rate either way.

options.text: It is a fault in the code that should be fixed
options.why: It is the rule working as designed. A falling $\varepsilon_t$ is the fix if you want less.

options.text: It has detected that an arm has changed
options.why: Plain epsilon-greedy detects nothing. It explores at the same rate whether or not arms change.

feedback.correct: The rate is fixed, so the cost never stops: that is the floor.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what the rule looks at when it decides to explore.

explain.text: Epsilon-greedy explores with chance $\varepsilon$ on every pull, whatever the estimates say. That gives the floor $\varepsilon(q^* - \bar q)$ per pull.
